column2: Pravrittaka is the entry of a character depending on that, or the stage-manager's speech where it is exactly the meaning of the line;
having taken it, the character enters — that is called Kathodghata. In applications, where the stage-manager describes an application,
and then the character enters, that is Prayogatishaya. The "body" of dramas and the like they call the plot (itivritta);
its two kinds are remembered as the established and the imagined. The established is seen in tradition; the imagined is created by the poet.
Seed (bija), drop (bindu), banner (pataka), episode (prakari) and the action itself — five elements of the plot, and five efforts in order:
beginning, effort, attainment, certainty, and the attainment of fruit — union with fruit is the fifth.
Opening (mukha), progression (pratimukha), womb (garbha), reflection (vimarsha) and conclusion (nirvahana) — in order the five junctures.
What is indicated in small measure and spreads in many ways, ending in the fruit, is called the seed.
Where the origin of the seed arises from various meanings and sentiments, following the body in the poem, that is declared the opening.
Arrangement of the desired matter, non-diminution of the account, attainment of passion in the performance and concealing of secrets,
described as wonderful, revelation of the revealed. As a man without limbs, so a poem is not excellent.
Without place and time no plot proceeds; therefore by the rule of taking those two the point is stated.

Of places, the land of Bharata; of times, the three ages beginning with Krita; without these two, the rise of happiness and sorrow of beings in places is nowhere. In a canto, news from the beginning of a canto, if brought in, is not a fault.
Bliss is innate in him; it is sometimes manifested. That manifestation of his is called the sentiment (rasa) of the wonder of consciousness.
The first modification of it is remembered as ego (ahankara); from that arises self-conceit, wherein this triple world ends.
From conceit arises love, which, attaining fullness, by commonality with transient feelings and the like is sung as the erotic (shringara).
Its divisions are the other sentiments, love, the comic and the rest, in many ways, with marks of sounds arising from special states of self and the like;
they arise from the continuum of qualities such as sattva from the Supreme Self. From passion arises the erotic; the furious from sharpness.
From joy and the like arises stammering of speech; voice-change from fear and the like. They hold mind-disturbance and grief from loss of the desired and the like;
anger is sharp awakening toward the hostile imitator; what is for completing human aims is called energy (utsaha).
Shaking from agitation of mind is declared trembling; discoloration, from despair and the like, is the reversal of luster;
water in the eyes from sorrow, joy and the like is famed as tears; setting of the senses, dissolution, from transgression and the like;
mind's weariness from detachment and the like is called despondency (nirveda); dejection arisen from mental pain and the like, exhaustion in the body;
apprehension is anticipation of coming evil; envy and jealousy; bewilderment of mind from use of intoxicants and the like is intoxication;
fatigue arising from excessive action, a weariness within the body; aversion to action such as love is called laziness of mind;
wretchedness is fall from sattva; anxiety is consideration of an object; failure to see the means of what is to be done is called delusion;
memory is reflection of an object experienced; judgment is determination of an object, brought by knowledge of truth;
shyness arisen from modesty, love and the like, a certain contraction of the mind; fickleness is instability; joy is clarity of mind;
possession, retaliation, sleeplessness, distress of the self; in a duty, failure of insight — is called dullness;
fortitude is the prosperity of increase from obtaining the desired; pride is contempt for others, feeling of superiority in oneself;
dejection is the frustration of fate and the like in a desired object; eagerness is trembling state from desire of the unattained;
stupor of the mind and senses, epilepsy is immobile state; in battle terror from fear of obstacles and the like; curiosity is amazement of mind;
non-calming of anger is impatience; awakening is the rise of consciousness; concealment is hiding by gesture and form;
from rage, harshness of heavy speech and punishment they know as fierceness; reasoning is conjecture; disease is mind's and body's obstruction;
madness is incoherent talk and the like from passion; by knowledge of truth and the like, the dissolving of mind's stains is supreme peace (shama).
Poets should employ the feelings and sentiments in poetry and the like. That by which love and the like is brought out,
is called a determinant (vibhava), twofold: of object and of stimulus; this group of feelings, love and the like, arises from it.
The object-determinant arises from the hero and the like: the steady-exalted, steady-arrogant, steady-playful,
and steady-peaceful — thus the hero is remembered fourfold; favorable, courteous, deceitful, brazen are the classes;
the pithamarda, vita and vidushaka — three; in the erotic, the hero's confidants are subsidiaries;
pithamarda, sambalaka, the glorious vita of his kind, the jester, the humorist: eight heroes and heroines.
Own wife, another's wife, and remarried — say the Kaushikas; the common one, not the remarried, and so on, in many divisions.
The stimulus-determinants stand through various refinements; those which kindle the feelings in the object-determinants;
the sixty-four arts, twofold by action and the like, by songs and the like; jugglery and memory — mostly the offering of laughter;
of the object-determinant by the awakened refined feelings; from memory, desire, aversion and effort of mind, speech, intellect and body,
the very beginning is remembered by the wise as the consequent (anubhava). It is experienced here and is stated.
What is mostly mental activity is called mental beginning; twofold, masculine and feminine, such is also famed.
Beauty, play, sweetness, steadiness, depth, gracefulness, generosity, splendor — eight are the masculine ones;
censure of the low, rivalry with the high, valor, skill and the like as causes; in the mind's nature there is beauty, as a house is adorned.
Bhava, hava, hela, shobha, kanti, dipti, madhurya, shaurya, pragalbhya, udarata,
sthairya, gambhirata — for women twelve determinants are told. Bhava, vilasa, hava: bhava is something born of joy;
the logic of speech is the beginning of speech, twelvefold: address (abhashana), converse (alapa), prattle (pralapa), much speech;
lament is speech of grief; repeated speech is anulapa; dialogue is utterance and reply; apalapa is speech otherwise;
news, departure, message, direction, exposition, essential instruction, application, pretext, description of another;
instruction, teaching words, pretended speech, naming — this activity is for awakening, the beginning of right understanding; its three kinds are style, mode and function.
The Latiya style has clear arrangement and not too brilliant an embodiment; though abandoned, it is told with many ornaments;
the mode that is even in actions: Bharati, Arabhati, Kaishiki and Sattvati — thus it is established fourfold.
Primarily speech, mostly men, with women, in Prakrit — because composed by Bharata it is called the Bharati style.
Bharati has four limbs: Vithi, Prahasana, Prastavana of plays and the like; and the Vithi limbs are thirteen:
Udghataka, Lapita the second, Asatpralapa, Vakshreni, Nalika, Vipana,
Vyahara, Timata, Chhalavaskandita, Ganda, Mridava, and the thirteenth Achita.
Prahasana is speech aimed at ridicule of ascetics and the like; Arabhati is remembered as full of magic, jugglery, battle and the like. Sankshiptaka, Pata and the raising of the matter...
No chief application anywhere, and that sometimes oblique. Akampita and Kampita, Dhuta and Vidhuta,
Parivahita, Adhuta, Avadhuta, Achita, Nikunchita, Paravritta, Utkshipta and Adhogata,
and Lalita — thus the head is to be known as thirteenfold. The brow-work is sevenfold: Patana, Bhrukuti, Mukha;
the glance is threefold: love, steady, transient, obstructive; with thirty-six divisions; the sentiment-born has eightfold there;
the eyeball action ninefold: whirling, moving and the like; the nose sixfold; the breath ninefold is held;
the lip work: sixfold; the chin action sevenfold; the face with turbidity and the like sixfold; the neck is remembered ninefold.
The hand is said to be mostly uncombined and combined: Pataka, Tripataka, and Kartarimukha,
Ardhachandra, Utkarala, Shukatunda, Mushti, Shikhara, Kapittha, Khetakamukha,
Suchyasya, Padmakosha, Shiras, Mrigashirsha, Kamulakalapadma, and Chatura, Bhramara,
Hamsasya, Hamsapaksha, Sandamsha, Mukula, Urnanabha, Tamrachuda — these twenty-four;
the uncombined hands are told; the combined are thirteen: Anjali, Kapota, Karkata, Svastika,
Katakavardhamana, Asanga, Nishadha, Dola, Pushpaputa, and Makara,
Gajadanta, Bahistambha, Vardhamana — other hands. The chest is fivefold: Abhugna, dancing and the like.
